name: The Canaanite woman
charge: Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table
summary: A woman of Canaan came out of the coasts of Tyre and Sidon crying after him for a daughter grievously vexed with a devil, and he answered her not a word. The disciples asked him to send her away, and he said he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; she came and worshipped and asked for help, and he told her it was not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to dogs. She agreed with him and asked only for the crumbs, and he called her faith great and healed the daughter from that hour.
offenseFull: Jesus departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, and a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts and cried after him, asking mercy of the son of David for a daughter grievously vexed with a devil (Matthew 15:21-22). The history class takes the name Canaan for the land and not for her nation: Tyre and Sidon stand in the land of Canaan, so calling her a woman of Canaan tells you where she lived. Mark gives her nation plainly: she was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, and she heard of him and came and fell at his feet (Mark 7:25-26). The class also marks what she called him. She said son of David, because everyone in that country knew he was born of a man out of a known line.

He answered her not a word. The disciples came and asked him to send her away because she cried after them, and he said that he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:23-24). The class presses the question that a reading of a messiah for all nations cannot answer: he was going through that country healing and teaching, so why would he not so much as speak to this woman, and why would his own disciples ask him to send her off. Then she came and worshipped him and said, Lord, help me (Matthew 15:25), and he told her to let the children first be filled, for it is not meet to take the children’s bread and cast it to the dogs (Matthew 15:26; Mark 7:27). The study notes mark the point exactly there: the order is stated plainly, and he does not soften it for her.
judgmentFull: She did not argue with the order; she asked inside it, saying that the dogs under the table eat of the children’s crumbs (Matthew 15:27; Mark 7:28). The class weighs what that admission was. Israel was told they were a holy people, chosen to be a special people above all people on the face of the earth (Deuteronomy 7:6), and the nations were counted as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance, as nothing before him (Isaiah 40:15-17). You never find an Israelite in the scriptures calling himself a dog. This woman did, and what she asked for was the dust of the balance, a crumb off the table.

Jesus answered that her faith was great and told her it would be to her as she would, and her daughter was made whole from that very hour (Matthew 15:28). Mark records that he sent her away on the strength of that saying, and that when she came to her house she found the devil gone out and her daughter laid upon the bed (Mark 7:29-30). The class marks both what she was commended for and what she was not given. She was not told to go and sin no more, and nothing was said to her about everlasting life. Set beside the woman of Samaria, who claimed Jacob as her father and was offered water springing up into everlasting life without even asking for it (John 4:12-14), the difference between the two answers is the difference between the two nations.

The class closes without malice in it. The crumb was still given; Christ showed her no hate, and the rule that follows for us is to live peaceably with all men as much as lies in us (Romans 12:18). The blessing did not come by overturning what he had said about the order of the house; it came to a woman who accepted the order and still believed mercy could reach her child. Matthew has already set down the only other faith commended in those words, and that was the centurion of Capernaum (Matthew 8:10).

text.text: Then Jesus went thence, and departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon.
And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.
For a certain woman, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, heard of him, and came and fell at his feet:
The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation; and she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter.
But he answered her not a word. And his disciples came and besought him, saying, Send her away; for she crieth after us.
But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
Then came she and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me.
But he answered and said, It is not meet to take the children’s bread, and to cast it to dogs.
But Jesus said unto her, Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children’s bread, and to cast it unto the dogs.
And she said, Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.
And she answered and said unto him, Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children’s crumbs.
For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God: the Lord thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth.
Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing.
And Lebanon is not sufficient to burn, nor the beasts thereof sufficient for a burnt offering.
All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity.
Then Jesus answered and said unto her, O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt. And her daughter was made whole from that very hour.
And he said unto her, For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter.
And when she was come to her house, she found the devil gone out, and her daughter laid upon the bed.
Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well, and drank thereof himself, and his children, and his cattle?
Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.
